chapter.title: Writing a filing system in C

section.title: Introduction
section.p: FileSwitch is the part of the RISC OS kernel that presents a single, consistent filing system interface to applications, and dispatches the individual operations that make up that interface to whichever filing system module currently owns the object being accessed. A filing system module is a normal relocatable module that registers a small table of entry points with FileSwitch; FileSwitch then calls those entry points directly, in SVC mode, with the parameters for each operation packed into registers.

Writing a filing system by hand, entirely in assembler, is possible but tedious: every entry point receives its parameters in different registers, using different reason codes, and the module must cooperate with FileSwitch's calling and error-reporting conventions exactly. This chapter describes a small, fixed layer - referred to below as the FSinC layer - that does that register-level work once, and re-presents each FileSwitch call to your code as an ordinary C function taking a pointer to a parameter structure. Writing a filing system in C then becomes a matter of filling in the bodies of eight C functions, plus a handful of small module-lifecycle routines, rather than hand-coding register-level dispatch.

This chapter is both a reference to the interface FileSwitch presents to a filing system module, and a recipe for turning the supplied template sources into a working filing system. It draws on the original Acorn "Making a Filing System for RISC OS in C" note, on the Filing Systems volume of the RISC OS Programmer's Reference Manual, and on the behaviour of the supplied template sources themselves.

section.title: Overview
section.p: A filing system module built with the FSinC layer is made up of three kinds of source:

item.p: An assembler veneer, common to every filing system built this way, that FileSwitch calls directly. It repackages FileSwitch's register-based call into a single parameter-block pointer, calls the matching C function, and repackages the C function's return value back into the registers and flags FileSwitch expects. You should not normally need to change this file.

A set of C source files, one per FileSwitch entry point, each containing a single function: fsentry_open in c._open, fsentry_getbytes in c._getbytes, fsentry_putbytes in c._putbytes, fsentry_args in c._args, fsentry_close in c._close, fsentry_file in c._file, fsentry_func in c._func, and fsentry_gbpb in c._gbpb. These are where your filing system's behaviour lives, and are the files you fill in.

A CMHG/CMunge module header that declares the module's name, SWI chunk, service calls, star commands and error blocks, and a small amount of C module-lifecycle code (initialisation, finalisation, service call and star command handling, and, if you need any, SWI handling).

Two further layers beneath the entry points, described in : a data layer (c.fsdata) that understands the structure of the medium, and a provider layer (c.provider, or c.testprov in the test build) that reads it. The entry-point files call down into the data layer, and the data layer calls down into the provider; neither of the lower layers knows anything about FileSwitch.

section.p: The template as supplied builds a filing system called DummyFS, whose eight entry-point functions accept every reason code they are offered but implement none of them: each case returns . DummyFS is a safe skeleton to build from: it declares itself to FileSwitch, can be selected with , and fails cleanly and predictably on every actual file operation until you replace the relevant cases with real behaviour. The production build has no medium (its provider reports none), so as supplied it answers every FileSwitch call with ; the test build, which carries a medium in memory, answers with instead, showing that the call reached the entry point.

Because a filing system module can be called for any object on any open handle at almost any time, and because RISC OS has no memory protection between modules, a filing system must be conservative in what it assumes about its environment. In particular, a filing system entry point is guaranteed only 1 KB of stack: do not declare large automatic variables, and do not write recursive filing system code.

subsection.title: Registering the module with FileSwitch
subsection.p:
A filing system does not need to poll for work, and it does not claim any vector. Instead, when your module initialises, it calls with reason
(FSControl_AddFilingSystem) and a pointer to an 11-word information block. This tells FileSwitch the filing system's name, its information word, and the address of each of the eight entry points described in .

Every address placed in the information block, and the address of the information block itself, must be given as an offset from the module's relocatable-module base (Image$$RO$$Base), not as an absolute address: FileSwitch stores these values and may call them at any later time, after the module has been relocated. Register R1 on entry to carries the current value of Image$$RO$$Base itself, so that FileSwitch can turn the stored offsets back into absolute addresses when it calls you.
The information block has the following layout:

offset-table.offset: offset to the filing system's name, a control-terminated string (also used as the argument to and )
offset to a friendlier, human-readable title string, used in banners and error messages
flags and filing system number describing the filing system, see below

subsection.p: The information word (word 8) is a bitfield:

bitfield-table.bit: the filing system's allocated number, unique among filing systems present on the machine; see

the largest number of files this filing system can easily have open at once, or 0 if there is no definite limit; used by system extensions such as the Font Manager to decide whether files may be left open
the filing system is read-only; see
an extra information word follows the block, at word 11
use for *Access, in preference to the attribute-writing reason codes
FileSwitch need not store directories for this filing system
pass & and % in paths when appropriate
the filing system supports the image filing system extensions
call whether or not the object exists
streams are interactive, so prompting for input is appropriate

subsection.p: Bits 16-23 are ignored by RISC OS 2. The template builds the word in h.consts from named parts (FilingSystemNumber, MaxOpenFiles and the InfoWord_* bits) so that each can be changed independently; the supplied filing system number is an example only, and must be replaced with your own allocation (see ) before the filing system is released, since FileSwitch rejects a registration whose number is already in use.

A filing system module must re-register itself whenever is issued, since this service call is FileSwitch's way of asking every filing system to re-announce itself, for example after a fresh call chain has been built following a module reinitialisation elsewhere in the system. The supplied module lifecycle code handles this for you already; you should not need to change it.

subsection.title: How FileSwitch calls an entry point
subsection.p: FileSwitch calls each of the eight entry-point addresses directly, in SVC mode, with interrupts enabled, passing the operation's parameters in registers R0 upwards (the exact registers used depend on the entry point and are described individually below), and the module's private word pointer in R12, exactly as for a SWI handler.

The supplied assembler veneer for each entry point saves R0-R7, then calls the matching C function with a single pointer, in R0, to that saved block of registers on the stack. Because the parameter structures in h.veneers are laid out so that each C structure field occupies the same word position as the corresponding incoming register, the C function can read and write the incoming parameters as ordinary structure fields, and the veneer copies any altered fields back into the outgoing registers when the C function returns.
On return from the C function:

item.p: A null return value (no error) leaves the V flag clear and copies the (possibly modified) parameter block back into R0-R7 for FileSwitch to read as the call's results.
A non-null return value is treated as a pointer to a standard RISC OS error block. The veneer places this pointer in R0 and sets the V flag, exactly as a SWI handler reporting an error would.

For specifically, the C bit on return also carries meaning, independently of any error: it is derived from whether R1 (the got_the_byte flag) is zero on return from the C function, and signals to FileSwitch whether a single unbuffered byte read reached end of file. See for details.

subsection.p: None of this register or flag manipulation is something your C code needs to implement directly: it is entirely the responsibility of the supplied veneer. It is described here because it explains why the parameter structures are shaped the way they are, and why some fields exist purely as padding - they correspond to registers that a particular call happens not to use.

subsection.title: Handles and identifiers
subsection.p: Two distinct handle types appear throughout the parameter structures. A FileSwitchHandle is the handle FileSwitch itself uses to identify an open file to the rest of the system (the value an application sees from ). A FileSystemHandle is a handle chosen and owned by your filing system, and returned from ; FileSwitch subsequently quotes this handle back to you on every other call concerning that open file, but never interprets it itself. You are free to use any representation for a FileSystemHandle that is convenient - an index into a private table of open files is a common choice - provided that zero is never returned as a valid handle.

category.title: Information_Fields
category.p: A number of entry points exchange a two-word field whose interpretation depends on context: for file load and save operations it holds a pair of RISC OS load and execute addresses (or, for filetyped files, the encoded filetype and datestamp packed into the load address); for datestamp queries it holds the two words of a low/high RISC OS 5-byte-plus timestamp pair. The type is defined as a C union so that either view can be used without an explicit conversion:
This structure is used directly by and .

category.title: YesNoAnswer
category.p: A number of fields are simple boolean flags, represented as a plain int typedef'd as YesNoAnswer, with the constants No (0) and Yes (any non-zero value, conventionally 1) defined for readability. Treat any non-zero value as "yes" when reading one of these fields back from a caller, rather than testing for the exact value 1.

subsection.title: Building a filing system from the template
subsection.p: The template's files divide into three groups: files you are expected to edit for every filing system, files you edit only to add module-level behaviour such as SWIs or extra star commands, and files you should normally leave alone. Working through the template to build a real filing system means:

item.p: Choose a module name, SWI chunk, service numbers and error base, and put them in the CMHG/CMunge header. The SWI chunk and error base supplied with the template are already in use by the example filing system they were extracted from, and must be replaced with values allocated to your own filing system before it is used outside of testing. When choosing the numbers for your own error blocks, try to match a similar error already generated by ADFS, so that programs which inspect error numbers after a file operation can recognise the same kind of failure regardless of which filing system raised it: for example, ADFS's "disc full" error is &108C6, and other filing systems' equivalents typically differ only in the two digits that encode the filing system number (NFS's is &121C6) - keep the low byte and the general shape of the number the same, and only change the filing-system-number digits.
Update the filing system name and information word in the constants header (h.consts in the template layout) to match your filing system.

Fill in the eight fsentry_* functions, described in below, one case at a time. Cases you have not yet implemented should continue to return (or a more specific error such as for reason codes your filing system will never support) rather than being left to fall through unhandled.

Replace the provider (c.provider) with code that reaches your real storage, and fill in the data layer (c.fsdata) with the code that reads your medium's structures; see . Keep the test provider (c.testprov) and its image up to date with your format, and extend tests.TestFS as each operation starts to work; see .

Fill in the module's initialisation, finalisation, service-call and star-command handling for anything specific to your filing system, such as responding to the arrival or removal of a medium, or offering additional star commands.

Add any private state your filing system needs - open-file tables, cached directory information, connection state and so on - as static data. Keep this as small and simple as you reasonably can: every byte of static data is permanently resident for as long as the module is, and a filing system with complex internal state is substantially harder to make robust against being called re-entrantly or during error recovery.

subsection.p: The assembler veneer, the CMHG/CMunge parameter-passing convention, and the C parameter-structure headers should not normally need to change: they implement the FileSwitch calling convention itself, which is fixed.

subsection.title: Structuring a filing system
subsection.p: The FileSwitch entry points are only the top of a filing system. Beneath them, a filing system has to understand the structure of what is on the medium, and beneath that it has to get bytes off the medium at all. The template separates these into three layers, and the separation is worth keeping as the filing system grows, because each layer changes for a different reason: the FileSwitch layer changes only when FileSwitch's conventions change (which is to say, almost never); the data layer changes when the on-medium format changes; and the provider layer changes when the storage the medium lives on changes.

definition-table.definition: Implements FileSwitch's register conventions, reason codes and error rules, and nothing else. Each entry point validates what FileSwitch gave it, asks the data layer for the object or data concerned, converts the answer into the registers FileSwitch expects, and returns. The open-file table (handles, sequential pointers) also lives here, since handles are a FileSwitch concept.

Understands the structure of the medium: where its root directory is, how directories and their entries are laid out, how names and dates are encoded, where an object's data lies. It presents every object as an fsdata_descriptor, and converts descriptors to RISC OS catalogue information. It also owns the volume state - whether a medium is mounted at all.

Reads ranges of bytes from the medium, and reports its size. It knows nothing about what the bytes mean. Only one provider is linked into any given module; the template supplies a production skeleton and an in-memory test provider.

subsection.p: The rule that makes the split useful is that each layer calls only the one below it, and nothing calls upwards: the FileSwitch layer calls fsdata_*, the data layer calls provider_*, and neither of the lower layers includes h.veneers or knows what a reason code is. A filing system built this way can be moved from one kind of storage to another by replacing one file, and its format handling can be tested without any hardware at all.

subsubsection.title: The provider layer
subsubsection.p: The provider interface is deliberately small. It is declared in h.provider as:

item.p: The context is opaque: its structure is defined inside the provider's own source file, and callers hold only a pointer to it. This is what allows the two providers to have entirely different state (a device handle and a sector buffer for real storage; a pointer and a length for the in-memory image) behind the same interface.

provider_read is a checked range read. An implementation must reject any range that does not lie entirely within the medium, and must fill the whole buffer or return an error - never a short transfer. Make the range check in the form offset > size || length > size - offset so that it cannot be defeated by the addition wrapping. The data layer relies on this: it can pass offsets straight from structures it has read off the medium, knowing that a corrupt or malicious value will be refused rather than read past the end of the device or of the image.
provider_size gives the data layer a known volume size against which to validate everything else it reads, before it reads it.
provider_open distinguishes "no medium" (, which is a normal state) from "cannot set up" (any other error, which stops the module loading). See .

subsubsection.p: The template addresses the medium in bytes, with a 32-bit offset, which is enough for media up to 4 GB. A filing system that must present something larger should change provider_offset to a block number and the units of provider_read and provider_size to blocks, and make the change in the data layer at the same time; nothing above the data layer is affected.

The provider is chosen at build time, and is never exposed through the FileSwitch entry points, a SWI or a *command. The production build links c.provider, which you replace with code that reaches your storage - for example through the BlockDevices interface, a podule driver, or a network connection. The test build links c.testprov, whose medium is a const image compiled into the module, and so is identical on every run. Both present the same interface, so the data layer cannot tell which it is talking to.

subsubsection.title: The data layer
subsubsection.p: The data layer's job is to turn "the bytes at offset N" into "the object called $.dir.leaf". It reads the medium's fixed structures once, at mount time, and then walks the directory structure on demand for each pathname it is given, describing each object it finds in an fsdata_descriptor: whether it is a directory, its length, its filetype and datestamp (or raw load and execution addresses, for a medium that records RISC OS metadata exactly), and its permissions, all in the medium's own terms.

Converting that description into what FileSwitch wants is the one place where the two vocabularies meet, and the template puts it in the data layer, as fsdata_to_riscos, rather than in c._file. Every entry point that reports an object - , , the records written by and its older forms, and the extent returned by - then reports it the same way, and the entry-point files never need to know how a date or a filetype is stored on the medium.

The datestamp is the RISC OS 5-byte count of centiseconds since 1 January 1900: its top byte goes into the low byte of the load address, and its low four bytes are the execution address. A medium that stores dates in another form (seconds since another epoch, a broken-down date) should convert them into this form when it fills in the descriptor, so that the conversion above stays fixed. A medium that stores no date at all should give the object a datestamp of zero and filetype &FFD (Data), unless the filing system can infer a better filetype from the name.

Permissions map onto the RISC OS attribute bits: owner read and write in bits 0 and 1, locked in bit 3, public read and write in bits 4 and 5. A medium with no concept of a particular permission should fill in the sensible default for it - readable, not locked, and writable only when the volume is writable - rather than leaving it unset.
A useful shape for an entry point that reports an object is then:

Note that "not found" is an error from the data layer's point of view but an object type of 0 from FileSwitch's; the entry point makes that translation, because it is a FileSwitch rule, not a format rule.

subsubsection.title: The no-medium state
subsubsection.p: A filing system module is loaded whether or not there is anything for it to present: the drive may be empty, the device not yet connected, the image not yet mounted. The template treats this as a normal state, the "no-medium" state, rather than a failure, and handles it in three places.

item.p: Initialisation. provider_open is called, and if it succeeds the volume is mounted with fsdata_mount. If it reports , the module carries on and still declares itself to FileSwitch; only some other error stops it loading. A filing system that fails to initialise because its medium is absent cannot be loaded from a boot sequence before the medium is present, which is usually the wrong behaviour.

The entry points. Every entry point that needs the medium asks fsdata_volume_present() first, and returns if there is none, before touching any structure that would not be there. The exceptions are , which must always release its handle (see below), and the reason codes that concern the filing system rather than the medium (, and ), which work without one. The result is that a *Cat DummyFS: on an empty drive gives a clean error, exactly as ADFS's "Drive empty" does, and nothing is left half done.

Removal. When the medium goes away while the module is running - an eject, a disconnection - whatever notices it (a service call from the device's driver, or a callback from the provider) calls fsdata_unmount(). That marks the volume absent first, then discards cached structures, then closes the provider, in that order, so that an entry point arriving part way through sees "no medium" rather than a half-released volume. Handles that were open on the medium stay in the open-file table; each subsequent operation on one of them fails with , and when FileSwitch eventually closes it, releases the table entry without needing the medium and without error. When a medium arrives again, the same provider_open and fsdata_mount sequence as at initialisation mounts it.

subsubsection.p: Finalisation is the mirror of initialisation, and its order matters. The module first removes the filing system with . FileSwitch calls for every file still open on the filing system as part of this, so the volume must still be mounted at that point for those closes to flush and complete normally. The module then frees any open-file table entries that the closes did not reach (there will be none unless FileSwitch itself was absent), and only then calls fsdata_unmount(), which closes the provider and releases the medium. The error from the removal is ignored: a module must never refuse to finalise because FileSwitch has been reinitialised underneath it.

subsubsection.title: Read-only filing systems
subsubsection.p: Many filing systems present a medium that is never written: a read-only disc, a distribution image, an archive. Such a filing system should set bit 16 (InfoWord_ReadOnly) of its information word, and answer every reason code that would modify the medium with . Everything else it implements normally. The following matrix lists every reason code by which side of that line it falls; the template's entry-point sources carry the same annotation against each case.

definition-table.definition: all (never reached, since no handle is opened for writing; return the error anyway)

definition.name: FSEntry_Args
definition.extra: 0, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9 (pointer, extent, allocation, EOF, flush, datestamp reads); 1 (WriteSequentialFilePointer) for a pointer within the extent

subsubsection.p: Two consequences are easy to miss. Directory enumeration and the directory-context reason codes are read operations, and a read-only filing system must implement them fully, or the Filer cannot show its contents; and is only a write when it would extend the file, so it should be implemented normally for any pointer up to the extent. When a descriptor is converted for a read-only volume, clear the write bits in the attributes it produces, so that applications which inspect attributes before offering to save see the object as it really is.

subsubsection.title: Allocations
subsubsection.p: Three numbers identify a filing system to the rest of the system, and all three in the template are examples only, not allocated to it or to any filing system built from it:

item.p: the SWI chunk base (swi-chunk-base-number in cmhg.modhead);
the error base (error-base in cmhg.modhead).

subsubsection.p: Each is unique across all RISC OS software, and each must be allocated to your filing system before it is released - together with the module name and the filing system name, which are likewise registered. Until then the example values are adequate for development, but two things follow from their being examples. First, another module built from the same template, or any module that happens to use the same values, cannot be loaded at the same time: FileSwitch refuses a second filing system with the same number or name, and two modules claiming the same SWI chunk will each dispatch the other's SWIs. Second, a filing system that re-implements an existing one - a replacement for a filing system already present in the ROM, presenting the same medium under the same name and number - cannot coexist with the original. It must either use its own name and number, and be a different filing system from the point of view of pathnames and applications, or it must be loaded in place of the original, with the original removed first.

When choosing error numbers within your allocated base, match the low byte of the equivalent ADFS error where one exists, as described in , so that software which inspects error numbers treats your errors as it treats ADFS's.

subsubsection.title: Matching an existing filing system's conventions
subsubsection.p: A filing system that presents a medium format which an existing RISC OS filing system also presents will be judged against that filing system: applications, and users, will expect the same pathnames to reach the same objects, with the same names, types and dates. The places where such a format's raw contents and RISC OS's view of them differ are the places where the two implementations can silently diverge, and each of them needs a deliberate decision, recorded in the data layer, and a test that pins the decision down. In particular:

item.p: Pathname separators. RISC OS uses . to separate path elements and / as an ordinary character, where most other formats do the reverse. Decide how the two are exchanged in each direction, and what happens to a name that contains both.

Filename conversion. Length limits, the character set, case folding, version or extension suffixes, and the characters RISC OS reserves ($ & % @ \ ^ : * # and the wildcards) all need a rule, and the rule needs to give the same leafname in directory enumeration as the one that fsdata_find will accept back.

Native metadata. A format may carry a RISC OS load and execution address, filetype or attributes in an extension record of its own; if the existing filing system honours that record, yours must recognise it in the same place and prefer it over anything inferred from the name.

Variant record lengths. A format with more than one variant - different sector or record sizes, or optional fields that change where an object's data starts - must have each variant's length handled by the provider or the data layer, and each variant represented in the test image.

Alternative name tables. A format that carries more than one directory tree (a base tree and a supplementary tree with longer or differently encoded names, for example) needs a rule for which is preferred, and for what happens when only one is present.

subsubsection.p: Each of these is a switch in the data layer, not in the FileSwitch layer, and each is a good candidate for a dedicated object in the test image and a check in tests.TestFS.

subsection.title: Testing
subsection.p: A filing system can only be tested by driving FileSwitch at it, since that is how every application reaches it; and FileSwitch can only reach a filing system that is registered, which needs a running RISC OS. The template therefore provides a test that is repeatable on any RISC OS, and is run automatically by the build service in CI:

item.p: A test build of the module, rm32.DummyFSTest, built by riscos-amu -f Makefile,fe1 ram TEST=1. It differs from the production module in one object only: the provider is c.testprov, whose medium is an image compiled into the module itself, rather than c.provider. Every run therefore sees exactly the same medium, and no hardware is needed. The test provider is private to this build: it is not a *command or SWI that can mount an image at run time in the production module, because anything that can be reached that way has to be supported and secured like any other feature.

A BASIC test program, tests.TestFS, which loads the test module, drives FileSwitch at it through , , and , and checks that each operation reaches the filing system and is answered as expected. It then loads the production module to check the no-medium behaviour, and reloads the test module to check re-registration. Each check prints PASS or FAIL, and a non-zero number of failures ends the program with an error, so that a build script sees a non-zero result.

subsection.p: Run the tests from the directory containing rm32:

p.extended-example: riscos-amu -f Makefile,fe1 ram riscos-amu -f Makefile,fe1 ram TEST=1 riscos-run --command "Run tests.TestFS"

subsection.p: or, on RISC OS itself, *Run tests.TestFS. Under Pyromaniac, filing system registration is governed by the Filesystem.register_filesystem configuration option, which is allow by default; a registered filing system appears under $.FS there, as well as through its own name: prefix.

As supplied, the tests check that each entry point is reached (by looking for ) rather than that it works. As you implement the filing system, each of those checks becomes a check on a real result - an object type of 1 for a file that the test image contains, the right bytes back from a read, the expected leafnames from an enumeration - and the test image in c.testprov grows the objects those checks need. Keep one object in the image for each convention described in , so that a change to a name or date rule is caught by a test rather than by a user.

section.title: Entry points
section.p: FileSwitch calls the following eight entry points. Each is documented below with the registers FileSwitch passes in, the registers it expects back, and, where the call is a multi-reason call, one definition per reason code. Reason codes not listed under a given entry point are not issued by FileSwitch for that entry point and should be rejected with if ever seen.

This section is a condensed, C-oriented restatement of the "Filing system interfaces" chapter of the RISC OS Programmer's Reference Manual, "Writing a filing system" (, with the FSEntry_Func 35-37 additions described separately in ). Each entry point and reason code below links to the matching section of that original document, which remains the canonical description; where the two disagree, the original document is correct.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Open
entry-definition.description: Open a file, directory, or other object for access

entry.register-use: reason code:
pointer to the object's full pathname, control-terminated
the FileSwitch handle that will identify this open file to the rest of the system; a small integer, typically counting down from 255, but must be treated as a full 32-bit word
pointer to any filing-system-specific "special field" text following the pathname, or 0 if none was given

exit.register-use:
information word for the opened object (not the same as the filing system's own information word):
the caller may write to this file the caller may not write to this file the caller may read this file the caller may not read this file the object opened is a directory the object opened is a file this filing system implements FSEntry_GBPB itself for this file, rather than relying on repeated single-byte GetBytes/PutBytes calls the stream behaves like an interactive device (for example a pipe) rather than a fixed-length file reserved, should be zero

the FileSystemHandle by which this filing system will subsequently identify this open file, chosen by the filing system itself; 0 means the open failed only because memory could not be allocated (this is not reported as an error - return NULL with R1 = 0)

the natural block size of the file (the same as the natural sector size for disc-based filing systems); FileSwitch aligns and sizes its transfers to multiples of this value. A value of 0 requests unbuffered transfers, one byte at a time, via and ; a non-zero value must be a power of two between 64 and 1024
current file extent (length in bytes); only meaningful when R2 is non-zero
space allocated to the file, a multiple of the buffer size, which may exceed the extent; only meaningful when R2 is non-zero

use.p: FileSwitch calls FSEntry_Open whenever an application opens a file on this filing system, for example via , or when the filing system's own housekeeping needs to open an object (for instance, opening a directory in order to read its contents). The reason code specifies the access mode requested.

The returned FileSystemHandle is opaque to FileSwitch: choose any non-zero representation that lets your other entry points find the corresponding open-file state again, such as an index into a private table of open files. FileSwitch will use this handle for every later call about this file, and expects your filing system to close every handle it still has open when *Close, *Shut, or is issued; FileSwitch calls once per handle itself, so a filing system does not need to implement "close everything" as a special case.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Open
entry-definition.description: Open an existing file for reading only

use.p: FileSwitch will already have checked that the object exists (unless the filing system set bit 28 of its own filing system information word to override this) before making this call. This reason code must not alter the object's datestamp.
Opening a directory for reading is valid, and is used by some programs purely to test whether an object exists; bytes will never actually be requested from a directory handle.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Open
entry-definition.description: Create a new file, or open an existing one, for reading and writing

use.p: FileSwitch will already have checked that the leafname is not wildcarded, and that the object is not an existing directory. If the file already exists, open it unchanged, for reading and writing. If it does not, create it: return an extent of zero; return an allocated space equal to that of a same-named file if one already existed, or a sensible default that leaves room to grow otherwise; give the new file filetype &FFD (Data), a current datestamp, and sensible access attributes (WR/ is recommended).

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Open
entry-definition.description: Open an existing file for reading and writing

use.p: FileSwitch will already have checked that the object exists and is not a directory before making this call. This reason code must not alter the object's datestamp.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_GetBytes
entry-definition.description: Read one byte, or a block of bytes, from an open file

entry.register-use: the FileSystemHandle returned from ; guaranteed not to be a directory
buffer address to read into; present only for a buffered (multiple-byte) transfer, not necessarily word-aligned
number of bytes to read; present only for a buffered transfer, and guaranteed to be a multiple of the buffer size returned from
file offset to read from; present only for a buffered transfer, guaranteed to be a multiple of the buffer size and within the file's extent

exit.register-use: for a single-byte unbuffered read, the byte read, in the low 8 bits

for a single-byte unbuffered read, a YesNoAnswer flag: zero if end of file was reached before a byte could be read, non-zero if a byte was read successfully; this is also reflected in the returned C flag (C set means end of file was reached)

use.p: This single entry point serves two distinct purposes, distinguished by whether the file was opened for buffered or unbuffered transfer (see the buffer size returned from ).

For a file opened buffered, FileSwitch calls this entry point to refill its own transfer buffer, either because a client called at an offset FileSwitch has no buffered data for, or because a client called to transfer a whole number of buffer-sized blocks and FileSwitch has chosen to have the filing system deliver the data straight into the client's memory (if FileSwitch had any modified, not-yet-flushed data in that range, it copies it into the client's memory itself immediately after this call returns). Your filing system should copy the requested bytes, starting at the given file offset, into the supplied buffer; the transfer routine's speed is important to overall filing system performance, so word-aligned copies should be optimised where possible.

For a file opened unbuffered (buffer size zero), FileSwitch calls this entry point once per byte read by the application, passing only the handle in R1; your filing system should return the next sequential byte from the file in R0, advancing the file's sequential pointer by one, unless the pointer is already at the end of the file, in which case return with the C flag set and R0 undefined. A filing system must not try to keep its own "EOF error on next read" flag - that is FileSwitch's responsibility - so it is enough to compare the sequential pointer with the extent on every call. If a filing system does not implement for unbuffered transfer, FileSwitch calls this entry point repeatedly to satisfy a multi-byte request, stopping as soon as C is returned set.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_PutBytes
entry-definition.description: Write one byte, or a block of bytes, to an open file

entry.register-use: for a single-byte unbuffered write, the byte to write, top 24 bits zero
the FileSystemHandle returned from ; guaranteed not to be a directory, and to have had write access granted at the time of the open
buffer address to write from; present only for a buffered (multiple-byte) transfer, not necessarily word-aligned
number of bytes to write; present only for a buffered transfer, and guaranteed to be a multiple of the buffer size returned from

file offset to write to; present only for a buffered transfer, guaranteed to be a multiple of the buffer size; the final byte written by the call is guaranteed to lie within the file's current extent, so the file never needs extending for a buffered write

use.p: This is the write counterpart to , called in the same two modes.

For a file opened buffered, FileSwitch calls this entry point either because a client called to write a whole number of buffer-sized blocks directly (discarding any modified-but-unflushed buffered data FileSwitch held in that range, since this call has just overwritten it), or because FileSwitch needs to flush one of its own modified buffers back to the file. Because the write is guaranteed to fall within the file's current extent, buffered writes never need to extend the file.

For a file opened unbuffered, FileSwitch calls this entry point once per byte written by the application, passing the byte to write in R0 and the handle in R1; write it at the file's current sequential pointer and advance the pointer by one. If the sequential pointer is equal to the file's extent when the call is made, the file must be extended by at least one byte to hold the new data - though it is more efficient to grow the allocation in larger chunks (256 bytes or 1 KB are typical) than one byte at a time. If a filing system does not implement for unbuffered transfer, FileSwitch calls this entry point repeatedly to satisfy a multi-byte request.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Miscellaneous operations on an open file

entry.register-use: reason code:
the FileSystemHandle returned from
arguments specific to the reason code, see below

exit.register-use: results specific to the reason code, see below

use.p: FSEntry_Args is a catch-all entry point for operations on an already-open file that do not fit or : moving the sequential file pointer, querying or changing the file's extent, flushing buffered output, and so on. Most reason codes correspond directly to .

Several reason codes below are documented as needed only by a filing system that supports unbuffered files (buffer size zero from ); a filing system that is always buffered can safely decline these with , since FileSwitch itself tracks the sequential pointer and EOF state for buffered files. Reason codes 3, 4, 7 and 9 are needed by every filing system, buffered or not.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Read the current sequential file pointer

exit.register-use: the current sequential file pointer, as a byte offset from the start of the file

use.p: Needed only for unbuffered files. If the concept of a sequential pointer is meaningless for this filing system (a keyboard stream, for example), return a pointer of 0 rather than an error.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Set the current sequential file pointer

entry.register-use: the new sequential file pointer, as a byte offset from the start of the file

use.p: Needed only for unbuffered files. If the new pointer is greater than the file's current extent: when the file was opened only for reading, or only read access was granted, return the error "Outside file"; otherwise extend the file with zero bytes and set its new extent to the new pointer, returning an error as soon as possible (and before updating the extent) if the file cannot be extended. If the concept of a sequential pointer is meaningless for this filing system, ignore the call rather than returning an error.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Read the current extent (length) of the file

exit.register-use: the file's current extent, in bytes

use.p: Needed only for unbuffered files. If the concept of a file extent is meaningless for this filing system, return an extent of 0 rather than an error.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Set the extent (length) of the file

entry.register-use: the new extent, in bytes

use.p: Needed by every filing system, whether buffered or not, but the two cases behave differently.

For a buffered file, FileSwitch only ever makes this call to fix the file's real length just before it is closed: simply record R2 as the object's new catalogued length, without otherwise touching the file's content.

For an unbuffered file, FileSwitch can make this call at any time on a client's request. If the new extent is less than the current sequential pointer, move the pointer in to match the new (smaller) extent. If the new extent is greater than the current one, extend the file with zero bytes, returning an error as soon as possible (and before updating the extent) if it cannot be extended. If the concept of a file extent is meaningless for this filing system, ignore the call rather than returning an error.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Read the amount of storage allocated to the file

exit.register-use: the space currently allocated to the file, in bytes, which may exceed its extent

use.p: Every filing system must support this reason code.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Test whether the sequential file pointer is at end of file

exit.register-use: -1 (all bits set) if the sequential pointer is equal to the file's current extent, or 0 otherwise; not a plain YesNoAnswer 0/1 value

use.p: Needed only for unbuffered files. If a filing system does not support a sequential pointer and/or file extent, because the concept is meaningless (a keyboard or null stream, for example), the treatment of this reason code is up to that filing system: for example, a keyboard device might signal EOF only when Ctrl-D is read, a null device might always signal EOF, and a VDU-output-style device might never signal EOF.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Flush any buffered output for this file to permanent storage

exit.register-use: a load_exec pair: the file's load and execute address, or 0/0

use.p: Only needed if the filing system does its own buffering on top of whatever FileSwitch already provides - for example read-ahead or write-behind caching, as ADFS does - and only called at all if the filing system set bit 27 of its own filing system information word when it registered itself. Write out any data your filing system is holding in its own buffers, in addition to anything FileSwitch itself asks for via .

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Ensure at least the given amount of storage is allocated to the file

entry.register-use: the amount of storage, in bytes, that must be available

exit.register-use: the amount of storage actually ensured, in bytes

use.p: Every filing system must support this reason code. Guarantee that at least this much storage can be allocated to the file without failing, without actually changing the file's extent or zeroing the extra space, so that a caller can pre-flight a large write before committing to it.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Write zero bytes into part of the file

entry.register-use: file offset at which to start writing zeros, a multiple of the buffer size
number of zero bytes to write, a multiple of the buffer size

use.p: Needed only for buffered files. The handle is guaranteed not to be a directory, and to have had write access granted at the time of the open.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Args
entry-definition.description: Read the file's datestamp

exit.register-use: load address of the file, with the bottom byte holding the most significant byte of the 5-byte datestamp, or 0 if the file cannot be datestamped from this handle
execution address of the file, holding the bottom four bytes of the 5-byte datestamp, or 0 if the file cannot be datestamped from this handle

use.p: Every filing system must support this reason code.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Close
entry-definition.description: Close a previously-opened file

entry.register-use: the FileSystemHandle returned from

a load_exec pair: new load and execute addresses to stamp on the file when closing, or 0/0. This is 0/0 whenever was itself called for this handle and returned 0/0 (meaning the file was never modified, or cannot be datestamped by handle); when it is non-zero, restamp the file with these values before closing

use.p: Flush any buffered data for this handle, release any resources associated with it (memory, open handles onto the underlying medium, entries in a private open-file table), and, if non-zero load and execute addresses were supplied, update the file's stored load and execute addresses to match before closing. The handle is invalid for any further FileSwitch call once this entry point returns successfully.

*Close and *Shut (close every open file) are both implemented by FileSwitch itself: it passes each of a filing system's open handles to this entry point in turn, one at a time, so a filing system does not need to implement "close everything" as a special case of its own.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Operations on a named file or directory that need not be open

entry.register-use: reason code:
pointer to the object's full pathname (wildcarded for several reason codes), control-terminated
meaning dependent on the reason code: usually a load_exec pair
meaning dependent on the reason code: either a length/attributes pair, or a start/end memory address pair for load and save
pointer to any filing-system-specific "special field" text following the pathname, or 0 if none was given

exit.register-use: object type: 0 (not found), 1 (file), 2 (directory), for reason codes that return catalogue information
a pair describing the object's load and execute addresses, for reason codes that return catalogue information
the object's length in bytes, for reason codes that return catalogue information
the object's access attributes, for reason codes that return catalogue information
pointer to the object's printable leafname, for reason codes that report one; FileSwitch copies this immediately, so it may point at a small static buffer

use.p: FSEntry_File handles whole-object operations identified by pathname rather than by an open handle: loading and saving a file in one call, creating or deleting an object, reading or writing its catalogue entry, and creating directories. It corresponds closely to .

Except where a reason code below says otherwise, do not return an error if the named object simply does not exist - return object type 0 (for reason codes that report a type) and otherwise take no action.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Save a block of memory as a new file

entry.register-use: load and execute addresses to give the new file
start address of the data to save
end address (exclusive) of the data to save

exit.register-use: pointer to a leafname for printing *Opt 1 info

use.p: FileSwitch has already validated the memory block and ensured the leafname is not wildcarded. If an object of this name already exists and is not locked, discard it first; the new file should have the same access attributes as the one it replaced, or a sensible default if there was none. Return an error such as "File locked" if the save cannot be done.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Set a file's load address, execute address and attributes together

entry.register-use: new load and execute addresses
new attributes

use.p: There is no length field for this reason code - length can only be changed via on an open file, or implicitly by . If the object is a directory, either write the information (FileCore-based filing systems do) or return an error - directories are not required to support this. Do not return an error if the object does not exist.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Set a file's load address

entry.register-use: new load address

use.p: If the object is a directory, either write the information or return an error. Do not return an error if the object does not exist.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Set a file's execute address

entry.register-use: new execute address

use.p: If the object is a directory, either write the information or return an error. Do not return an error if the object does not exist.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Set a file's access attributes

entry.register-use: new attributes

use.p: Do not return an error if the object does not exist.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Read a file's full catalogue entry, including its length

exit.register-use: object type: 0 (not found), 1 (file), 2 (directory)
load and execute addresses
length
attributes

use.p: Return an error only if the pathname names an unknown drive or media, or an unknown server/subsystem in the special field. Return object type 0, not an error, if the containing directory exists but no object in it matches the leafname, or if the containing directory itself does not exist.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Delete a file or an empty directory

exit.register-use: object type of the object that was deleted
the load and execute addresses the object had before deletion
the length the object had before deletion
the attributes the object had before deletion

use.p: FileSwitch has already ensured the leafname is not wildcarded. Return an error if the object is locked against deletion, but not if it simply does not exist. No data is transferred for this call; the returned values describe the object as it was immediately before deletion.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Create a new file from a block of memory, without transferring its data

entry.register-use: load and execute addresses to give the new file
start address in memory
end address in memory, plus one

exit.register-use: pointer to a leafname for printing *Opt 1 info

use.p: R4 and R5 are used only to calculate the length of the file to create - unlike , no data is transferred from that memory range. If an object of this name already exists and is not locked, discard it first; the new file should have the same access attributes as the one it replaced, or a sensible default if there was none. Return an error if the file could not be created.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Create a new, empty directory

entry.register-use: load address (ignored under RISC OS 2)
execute address (ignored under RISC OS 2)
a hint for the number of entries the directory should be sized for, or 0 for a sensible default, which a filing system without fixed-size directories may ignore

use.p: FileSwitch has already ensured the leafname is not wildcarded. If the directory already exists, either leave it unmodified, or attempt to rename it out of the way (an error from that rename attempt must not be passed back). If directories on this filing system cannot hold separate load/execute addresses (only a directory type/datestamp), simply ignore R2 and R3 rather than returning an error. Return an error if the directory could not be created.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Read a file's catalogue entry, but not its length

exit.register-use: object type
load and execute addresses
attributes

use.p: As , but R4 need not be filled in; provided because computing a length can be expensive for some filing systems (this is particularly useful for a network filing system whose server does not store length in the directory itself). This reason code is only issued by *Copy under RISC OS 2, and only if the filing system set bit 26 of its information word at initialisation; otherwise FileSwitch calls and ignores the length it returns. Do not return an error if the object does not exist.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_File
entry-definition.description: Load a whole file into memory

entry.register-use: pointer to the object's full pathname, possibly wildcarded

address to load the file at; always a concrete address, since FileSwitch resolves the "load at the file's own stamped address" case itself, using the load/execute addresses it read with , before making this call

exit.register-use: corrupted; do not rely on any particular value
the load and execute addresses the file was stamped with
the file's length
the file's attributes
pointer to the object's non-wildcarded, printable leafname (for example, if R1 named $.!b* and the boot file was matched, this should point to !Boot)

use.p: FileSwitch will already have called and validated the request before making this call: it will already have reported "File not found" or "'x' is a directory" as appropriate, run any load action associated with the object's filetype (which may itself recurse back into loading the file), reported "Access violation" if read access was not granted, and reported "No writeable memory at this address" if the destination was not valid. Unless the filing system talks to a multi-user server such as NetFS, where the object could change between calls, the object being loaded here is still the one whose catalogue entry was read moments earlier.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Directory, path and filing-system-wide operations

entry.register-use: reason code, see below
meaning dependent on reason code, see below

exit.register-use: meaning dependent on reason code, see below

use.p: FSEntry_Func is the largest and most varied entry point: it covers everything that does not belong to an individual open file, including setting the current and library directories, listing a directory's contents, examining or renaming objects by wildcard, setting access attributes, reading and writing filing-system-wide options, and handling filing-system shutdown. Many reason codes correspond directly to a star command or SWI available to applications.

Many reason codes below are described as being "called by RISC OS 2; otherwise only called if" some bit of the filing system information word (or its extra word) is set. This reflects a change in FileSwitch after RISC OS 2: newer versions of FileSwitch implement several of these operations themselves, using more primitive calls such as , and only fall back to calling the filing system directly if it advertises that it wants to handle the operation itself. A minimal filing system, targeting RISC OS 3 or later, can leave the corresponding information word bits clear and need not implement those reason codes at all - though it must still support reason codes that are always called, such as 0, 1 (RISC OS 2 only), 7, 8, 9, 10, 14 and 16.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Set the current directory

entry.register-use: pointer to the new current directory's pathname, possibly wildcarded, or NULL to mean the user root directory

use.p: Always called by RISC OS 2; on later versions, only called to implement *Opt 1 when bit 23 of the filing system information word is clear. Do not also make the new directory the current context (in the sense of a logged-on server or similar) as part of this call - provide a separate mechanism for that, such as a *FS-style command.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Set the library directory

entry.register-use: pointer to the new library directory's pathname, possibly wildcarded, or NULL to mean this filing system's own default

use.p: Only called by RISC OS 2. Do not also make the new directory the current context as part of this call, for the same reason as .

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Produce a *Cat-style listing of a directory

entry.register-use: pointer to a wildcarded directory name, or NULL to mean the current directory

use.p: Write a directory listing directly to the current output stream, in the same style as the *Cat command. Always called by RISC OS 2; on later versions, only called if bit 1 of the extra filing system information word is set.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Produce a *Ex-style listing of a directory

entry.register-use: pointer to a wildcarded directory name, or NULL to mean the current directory

use.p: Write full information on every object in the named directory directly to the current output stream, in the same style as the *Ex command (compare , which lists names only). Despite its name in this template, this reason code is not a query for the current directory's own name - see for that. Always called by RISC OS 2; on later versions, only called if bit 2 of the extra filing system information word is set.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Produce a *LCat-style listing of a directory relative to the library directory

entry.register-use: pointer to a wildcarded directory name relative to the library directory, or NULL to mean the library directory itself

use.p: Write a directory listing directly to the current output stream, in the same style as the *LCat command. Always called by RISC OS 2; on later versions, only called if bit 1 of the extra filing system information word is set.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Produce a *LEx-style listing of a directory relative to the library directory

entry.register-use: pointer to a wildcarded directory name relative to the library directory, or NULL to mean the library directory itself

use.p: Write full information on every object in the named directory directly to the current output stream, in the same style as the *LEx command. Despite its name in this template, this reason code does not return the library directory's own name - see for that. Always called by RISC OS 2; on later versions, only called if bit 2 of the extra filing system information word is set.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Produce a *Info-style listing for a set of objects

entry.register-use: pointer to a wildcarded pathname

use.p: Write full information on every matching object directly to the current output stream, in the same format as uses (this corresponds to the *Info command). Always called by RISC OS 2; on later versions, only called if bit 2 of the extra filing system information word is set.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Set filing-system-wide options

entry.register-use: the option number to set, or 0 to reset every option to its default value
the new value for that option

use.p: This corresponds to the *Opt command. Option number 1 is never passed to a filing system, since FileSwitch maintains it itself; option number 4 sets the boot file action (see ). Other option numbers are free for a filing system's own use, though a distinct allocation should be sought before shipping a real filing system using one. Return an error for a bad combination of option number and value.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Rename or move an object, possibly with wildcards

entry.register-use: pointer to the source pathname, possibly wildcarded
pointer to the destination pathname

exit.register-use: 0 if the rename was performed; non-zero if it could not be done as a "simple" rename (for example, because the two names are on different discs) - FileSwitch will then report "Bad rename" to the caller itself

use.p: This corresponds to the *Rename command.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Set access attributes on a set of objects, possibly with wildcards

entry.register-use: pointer to a wildcarded pathname
pointer to the access attribute string to apply, terminated by a null, space, or control character

use.p: This corresponds to the *Access command. Ignore any owner-access bits that are not applicable to this filing system, but still try to store the public-access bits. Always called by RISC OS 2; on later versions, only called if bit 18 of the filing system information word is set.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Perform *Opt 4-style boot handling for this filing system

use.p: For example, ADFS examines the boot option (as set by *Opt 4) of the disc in the configured drive and acts on it - option 2 runs &.!Boot - while NetFS attempts to log on as the configured boot user. This call may not return, if it ends up running an application.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Read the name and boot option of the currently-selected medium

entry.register-use: pointer to a buffer to receive the data; not pre-validated by FileSwitch, since it does not know how big the buffer needs to be - validate it yourself, and return "No writable memory at this address" (RISC OS 2) or the token BadWrt (later versions) if it is not usable. Do not lock/interlock this memory while writing to it

use.p: Write a length-prefixed disc name followed by a boot option byte into the buffer, as a single byte holding the name's length, that many bytes of name, then the boot option byte. If there is no current medium (no CSD), return the name "Unset" and a boot option of 0.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Read the current directory's name together with its access privilege

entry.register-use: pointer to a buffer to receive the data; not pre-validated by FileSwitch - validate it yourself, and return "No writable memory at this address" if it is not usable

use.p: Write a zero byte, then a length-prefixed current directory name, then a privilege byte, into the buffer: &00 if the caller has "owner" status in that directory (may create and delete objects there), or &FF for "public" status (may not). FileCore-based filing systems always report owner status. If there is no current directory, return the name "Unset". Only called by RISC OS 2.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Read the library directory's name together with its access privilege

entry.register-use: pointer to a buffer to receive the data; not pre-validated by FileSwitch - validate it yourself, and return "No writable memory at this address" if it is not usable

use.p: Write a zero byte, then a length-prefixed library directory name, then a privilege byte, into the buffer, in the same format as . If there is no library directory selected, return the name "Unset". Only called by RISC OS 2.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Read a block of directory entry leafnames

entry.register-use: pointer to the directory's pathname, possibly wildcarded, or 0 for the current directory (or the root directory, for an image filing system)
pointer to a buffer to receive leafnames
maximum number of entries to return
index of the first entry to read (an opaque continuation value, 0 to start at the beginning of the directory)
buffer length in bytes

exit.register-use: number of entries actually returned
the index to pass next time to continue reading, or -1 if there are no more entries

use.p: Write the matching leafnames into the buffer as consecutive null-terminated strings; never overflow the buffer, and only count a name once it has been written in full. Return an error if the directory itself is not found, or is a file rather than a directory. Because the buffer's validated length depends on whether the original call was (only [R3] 10-character entries plus terminators are guaranteed valid) or (the whole R2/R5 range is valid) and a filing system cannot tell which was used, write conservatively as though only the smaller guarantee applies. It is valid to return zero entries with R4 = -1, both when the buffer was too small to hold even one entry, and when the previous call's last entry exactly reached the end of the directory.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Read a block of directory entries together with their catalogue information (RISC OS 2/3 record format)

entry.register-use: pointer to the directory's pathname, possibly wildcarded, or 0 for the current directory
pointer to a buffer to receive records
maximum number of entries to return
index of the first entry to read (an opaque continuation value, 0 to start at the beginning of the directory)
buffer length in bytes

exit.register-use: number of records actually returned
the index to pass next time to continue reading, or -1 if there are no more entries

use.p: As , but each buffer entry is a fixed-size, word-aligned record rather than a bare name:

Round the buffer pointer up to a word boundary before writing each record (for example with ADD r2,r2,#3 followed by BIC r2,r2,#3). Return an error if the directory itself is not found, or is a file rather than a directory.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Prepare for the machine to be shut down or reset

use.p: Go into as dormant a state as possible - for example, park hard drive heads in their transit position. FileSwitch will already have closed every open file on this filing system before making this call.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Print a start-up banner describing the current directory when this filing system is selected

use.p: Called on a reset service call when the filing system's title-string offset (word 1 of the filing system information block) is -1, so that the banner text can vary - for example, "Acorn Econet" versus "Acorn Econet no clock". Print the banner with an XOS_... SWI (so that any error it raises is reported normally, with V set and R0 pointing at an error block, though this is unlikely in practice).

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Never called by FileSwitch

use.p: This reason code is defined but never issued by FileSwitch. A filing system does not need to implement it, beyond returning like any other reason code it does not recognise.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Read a block of directory entries and full catalogue information (RISC OS 3+ record format)

entry.register-use: pointer to the directory's pathname, possibly wildcarded, or 0 for the current directory
pointer to a buffer to receive records
maximum number of entries to return
index of the first entry to read (an opaque continuation value)
buffer length in bytes

exit.register-use: number of records actually returned
the index to pass next time to continue reading, or -1 if there are no more entries

use.p: A revised, RISC OS 3-and-later form of , used for reason codes 9 and 10, with a differently-shaped word-aligned record:

offset-table.offset: centiseconds since 1 Jan 1900, or 0 if the object is not datestamped

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_Func
entry-definition.description: Produce a *FileInfo-style listing for a set of objects

entry.register-use: pointer to a pathname, wildcarded only under RISC OS 2

use.p: Write full information on the given object (or, under RISC OS 2, every object matching a wildcarded pathname) directly to the current output stream, in the same format as the *FileInfo command. Only called if bit 25 of the filing system information word was set at initialisation; otherwise FileSwitch synthesises the same output itself using repeated calls.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_GBPB
entry-definition.description: Transfer multiple bytes to or from an open, unbuffered file

entry.register-use: reason code:
the FileSystemHandle returned from
buffer address to transfer to or from
number of bytes to transfer
file offset to transfer at, for the "here" reason codes (1 and 3) only; not supplied on entry for reason codes 2 and 4, which use the file's own sequential pointer instead

exit.register-use: address of the byte after the last one actually transferred to or from the buffer
number of bytes not transferred (zero if the whole transfer completed)
the file offset the transfer started at, plus the number of bytes actually transferred

use.p: This entry point exists so that a filing system able to transfer many bytes in one operation is not forced through the byte-at-a-time / interface. It is only called if set bit 28 (unbuffered GBPB supported) in the returned information word for this file; a filing system that does not set that bit need not implement this entry point at all, since FileSwitch will instead call / the necessary number of times itself. It corresponds to reason codes 1-4 for an already-open file.

reference.name: Get/put bytes from/to an unbuffered file

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_GBPB
entry-definition.description: Write multiple bytes at a given file offset

use.p: If the given file offset lies beyond the file's current extent, fill the gap with zero bytes before writing the new data, extending the file as necessary.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_GBPB
entry-definition.description: Write multiple bytes at the file's current sequential pointer

use.p: As , but at the file's own sequential pointer rather than an explicit offset; R4 is not given on entry.

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_GBPB
entry-definition.description: Read multiple bytes from a given file offset

use.p: If the given file offset is at or beyond the file's current extent, transfer nothing: do not update the sequential pointer, and do not return an error (FileSwitch derives the C flag it reports to its own caller from whether R3 is left non-zero, so no explicit EOF signalling is needed here).

entry-definition.name: FSEntry_GBPB
entry-definition.description: Read multiple bytes from the file's current sequential pointer

use.p: As , but at the file's own sequential pointer rather than an explicit offset; R4 is not given on entry.

section.title: Service calls
section.p: A filing system module handles the following service call.

service-definition.name: FSRedeclare
service-definition.description: All filing systems should re-declare themselves to FileSwitch

entry.register-use: &hex;40 (reason code)

use.p: FileSwitch issues this service call to ask every currently active filing system to call again, exactly as it did during initialisation. A filing system module must claim this service call and re-register itself in response; otherwise it can be left unreachable after certain module reinitialisation sequences elsewhere in the system.

section.title: Error messages
section.p: The template declares the following errors. Only belongs to the template itself; the others are commonly needed by any real filing system and are provided as a starting point. Their numbers follow from the example error base in cmhg.modhead, and change with it; see .

use.p: Report this when an operation cannot be completed because memory (RMA, workspace, or a private buffer) could not be claimed.

Returned by the supplied template code for any reason code an entry point's switch statement does not recognise. Because FileSwitch only ever issues reason codes documented in , seeing this error normally indicates a mismatch between the module and the version of FileSwitch calling it, rather than a caller error.

error-definition.name: DoesNothing
error-definition.description: This dummy filing system does nothing

use.p: Returned by every unimplemented case in the template's fsentry_* functions. A finished filing system should not return this error for any reason code it actually expects to receive in normal use; replace each case with real behaviour, or with a more specific and meaningful error, as you implement the corresponding functionality.

Returned by every entry point that needs the medium when no volume is mounted: before a medium has been inserted or connected, after one has been removed, and by the production build of the template as supplied, whose provider has no medium. See .

Returned by a read-only filing system from every reason code that would modify the medium; see for which those are. Also appropriate for a writable filing system whose medium is currently protected against writing by hardware.

section.title: *Commands
section.p: The template provides a single star command, which every filing system built from it should rename to match the filing system's own name.

command-definition.name: DummyFS
command-definition.description: Select DummyFS as the current filing system

use.p:
Selects this filing system as the current filing system, exactly as *ADFS or *NET do for their own filing systems. Internally this calls
(FSControl_SelectFilingSystem) with the filing system's registered name.

subsection.title: Implementing unbuffered reads
subsection.p: The following sketch shows how might be implemented, in c._getbytes, for a filing system that keeps each open file as a single contiguous block in memory, addressed through a private open-file table indexed by the FileSystemHandle:

Note that the same union is used for both the incoming parameters (getbytes_definition) and the outgoing result (getbytes_result): the handle read from parm->getbytes_definition.handle at the start of the function is at the same address as parm->getbytes_result.byte_got that is written at the end, so read every field you need from the incoming parameter block before you start writing the outgoing result into it.

subsection.title: Declaring a filing system with a fresh SWI chunk and error base
subsection.p: Before any filing system built from this template is used outside of testing, its CMHG/CMunge header must be given values that are actually allocated to it, not the placeholder values copied from the example this template was extracted from:

swi-chunk-base-number: your allocated SWI chunk
error-base: &your allocated error base
